name: Yogācāra
regions: Gandhāra and Ayodhyā (tradition's account of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu)

tradition.text: Taught by Maitreya to Asaṅga in the Tuṣita heaven; propagated by Asaṅga and his half-brother Vasubandhu

scholarly.text: Yogācārabhūmi material from c. 3rd–4th c. CE; Asaṅga and Vasubandhu c. 4th–5th c. CE; Indian Yogācāra active to the 12th c.

transmissions_received.what: the abhidharma framework of dharmas, mental factors and the path (the Abhidharmasamuccaya re-works it)
seeds (bīja) and the series (santāna); momentariness; the image-bearing cognition
the bodhisattva path, the perfections, emptiness of the Prajñāpāramitā read through the three natures

transmissions_given.what: the Cheng weishi lun system via Xuanzang and Kuiji
mind-only as a stage on the way to emptiness (Śāntarakṣita, Kamalaśīla)
the ālaya / tathāgatagarbha relation (Laṅkāvatāra; Ratnagotravibhāga as a Maitreya text)
the Laṅkāvatāra and mind-only teaching (the 'Laṅkā masters')
the three natures read as other-emptiness (shentong)
the idealist critique of external objects, used and transformed by Utpaladeva

distinctive_positions: The three realms are cognition-only (vijñaptimātra): what appears as an external object is cognition appearing as an object (Viṃśatikā 1; Triṃśikā 17).
Eight kinds of consciousness: six operative consciousnesses, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas) and the store-consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna) holding all seeds (Triṃśikā 2–16; Mahāyānasaṃgraha ch. 1).

Three natures (trisvabhāva): the imagined, the dependent and the perfected; and the three naturelessnesses by which the Prajñāpāramitā's 'all dharmas are without own-being' is to be understood (Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 6–7; Triṃśikā 20–25).
Unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) exists; the duality of grasped and grasper does not; emptiness exists in it (Madhyāntavibhāga 1.2).
Liberation is the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), the store-consciousness turning into mirror-like wisdom and the other consciousnesses into the other three wisdoms.
Beings belong to different spiritual lineages (gotra), some with no lineage for liberation (Bodhisattvabhūmi; Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ch. 3) — a thesis later Mahāyāna authors contested.
The yogin's path of calm and insight is mapped in detail: nine stages of settling the mind, seven attentions, four kinds of meditation object (Śrāvakabhūmi).
summary: The 'practice of yoga' school of Indian Mahāyāna, founded (in its own account) on the revelation of the bodhisattva Maitreya to Asaṅga and systematized by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. It teaches that the world as experienced is the unfolding of cognition from the seeds in the store-consciousness, analyses experience through the three natures, and maps the path from calm and insight to the transformation of the basis and buddhahood with its four wisdoms and three bodies.

name: Buddhist epistemology and logic (pramāṇa school)
alt_names: the school of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti
Buddhist logicians (bauddha naiyāyika in opponents' texts)
regions: South India and Kāñcī (tradition's account of Dignāga)

scholarly.text: Dignāga c. 480–540; Dharmakīrti c. 6th–7th c.; the school active in India until the late 12th c. and continued in Tibet

transmissions_received.what: mind-only, self-awareness and the ultimate non-duality of cognition
the vocabulary and genre of debate, the members of proof, points of defeat — critically revised

transmissions_given.what: the challenge that reshaped Nyāya (Uddyotakara, Vācaspati, Udayana answer Dignāga and Dharmakīrti)
the categories and arguments Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta engage and invert
a logic culture engaged by Akalaṅka, Haribhadra, Prabhācandra
the tshad ma curriculum and the Collected Topics (bsdus grwa)

distinctive_positions: There are exactly two means of valid cognition — perception and inference — because there are exactly two kinds of object, the unique particular and the universal (PS 1.2; NB 1.2–3, 1.12–17).
Perception is free of conceptual construction and non-erroneous (NB 1.4); it has four kinds: sensory, mental, reflexive self-awareness and yogic (NB 1.7–11).

A valid reason has three characteristics (trairūpya): present in the subject, present only in similar cases, absent from all dissimilar cases (NB 2.5); there are three kinds of valid reason — effect, own-nature and non-perception (NB 2.11).
Words and concepts do not reach real universals; they operate by exclusion of the other (anyāpoha).
Whatever exists is momentary, since to exist is to be causally efficacious (Ratnakīrti: yat sat tat kṣaṇikam).
Every cognition is reflexively aware of itself (svasaṃvedana); the result of a means of knowledge is this self-awareness.

The Buddha is a 'person of valid cognition' (pramāṇabhūta) because he knows what is to be abandoned and adopted with its means, a knowledge born of compassion cultivated over many lives (PV Pramāṇasiddhi chapter).
No creator god, no authorless scripture, no permanent self: each is refuted by reasoning.
summary: The Buddhist tradition of logic and epistemology founded by Dignāga and recast by Dharmakīrti, which recognized only perception and inference, grounded all reasoning in causal efficacy and momentary particulars, explained language by exclusion, and used this apparatus both to defend the Buddha's authority and liberation and to refute self, God and the authority of the Veda. Its Indian line ended with the monasteries of Bengal and Bihar; it lives on in the Tibetan monastic curriculum.

name: Satyākāravāda (True-Aspect Yogācāra)
distinctive_positions: The images (ākāra) that appear in cognition are real as cognition itself; the manifold image is one non-dual variegated cognition (citrādvaita).
Only the duality of grasped and grasper, not the images themselves, is false.
summary: A late Indian Yogācāra position (and Tibetan doxographic class) holding that cognition's appearing aspects are real; associated especially with Jñānaśrīmitra and Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla.
notes: The division into 'true' and 'false' aspect is partly a later doxographic construction (Tibetan grub mtha'); Indian authors use sākāra/nirākāra with shifting meanings. Membership lists are the doxographers'.

name: Alīkākāravāda (False-Aspect Yogācāra)
distinctive_positions: The images appearing in cognition are false (alīka), superimposed by beginningless imprints; only the luminous, image-free cognition is real.
In meditation and at buddhahood cognition is without any image.
summary: A late Indian Yogācāra position (and Tibetan doxographic class) holding that the appearing aspects of cognition are unreal and only pure self-luminous awareness is real; defended above all by Ratnākaraśānti.
notes: As with lin:satyakaravada, the classification is largely Tibetan doxographic; Ratnākaraśānti presents his view as the meaning of Madhyamaka too, and later Tibetan authors (Jonang) read the Maitreya texts in a related way.

name: Dilun school (Chinese 'Daśabhūmika treatise' school)

scholarly.text: 6th c. CE; absorbed into Huayan by the 7th c.

transmissions_given.what: the study of the Daśabhūmika and the nature of the ālaya

distinctive_positions: Founded on Vasubandhu's commentary on the Daśabhūmika translated by Bodhiruci and Ratnamati (508–511).
Split (as usually reported) into a northern branch holding the ālaya to be defiled and a southern branch (Huiguang) identifying the pure aspect of the ālaya with true suchness / buddha-nature.
summary: An early Chinese Yogācāra-derived exegetical tradition centred on Vasubandhu's Daśabhūmika commentary, later absorbed into Huayan.

name: Shelun school (Chinese 'Mahāyānasaṃgraha' school)

scholarly.text: founded on Paramārtha's translation of the Mahāyānasaṃgraha (563); absorbed into Faxiang in the 7th c.

transmissions_given.what: a body of Yogācāra exegesis superseded by Xuanzang's translations

distinctive_positions: Studied Asaṅga's Mahāyānasaṃgraha in Paramārtha's version.
Taught (following Paramārtha) a ninth, 'stainless consciousness' (amalavijñāna) beyond the ālaya, identified with suchness.
summary: The Chinese tradition of studying Paramārtha's translation of Asaṅga's Mahāyānasaṃgraha, notable for the doctrine of a ninth, pure consciousness; superseded by Xuanzang's Faxiang.

name: Hossō school (Japanese Faxiang)

scholarly.text: transmitted to Japan from 653 (Dōshō) onward; one of the six Nara schools; continues at Kōfukuji and Yakushiji

distinctive_positions: The Cheng weishi lun system of eight consciousnesses and five gotras, as transmitted from Xuanzang and Kuiji.
summary: The Japanese continuation of the Chinese Faxiang (Yogācāra) school, one of the six Nara schools, still maintained at Kōfukuji and Yakushiji.
notes: Scope overlaps U54 (Faxiang) and U55 (Japan); created here because no unit owns it.
